Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

Another SaaS sell off is just inevitable at this point because of the rise of AI agents.

Goldman Sachs expects the software profit pool to shift heavily toward AI agents, with the agent market growing to more than $50 billion by 2030 while traditional SaaS falls from roughly $30 billion to around $20 billion.

It also weakens customer lock in because users become more loyal to the agent than to the software it operates.

Yes, I know many large software companies now offer usage based pricing alongside their legacy seat based models. That should help them adapt as customers move toward paying for completed work rather than software access but the market rarely makes that distinction during a major sell off. If investors begin dumping SaaS stocks because they fear AI agents will weaken seat growth and pricing power, even the strongest software giants will probably get grouped into the same trade and sold alongside the weaker companies. And once Muse, OpenAI and Anthropic begin competing to control the user’s entire workflow, SaaS companies will no longer compete only against other software products but also compete against the AI agents deciding which software gets used in the first place.

Not every SaaS company will lose because those with proprietary data, deep integrations and strong usage based models should be more defensible but if another broad SaaS sell off begins, the market may not care about those differences at first. I’ve interviewed for these companies (sometimes more than once) over the past ~5 years. Got to the offer stage in 4 of them, and ended up working for 2.

This is a summary of my experience, top-down in classic MBB fashion👇🏼

All of these companies share these factors in how they filter talent:

Target schools, 90% GPA, extracurricular activities, experience (for non entry-level roles) and Case-interview performance. You don’t need all of them to get in, but you need to tick at least 3 of these boxes.

1. Target schools: 

The most controversial one, there is no real definition for this, it changes by firm, and by office within the same firm. But generally it looks something like this:

a) Top 30 schools in NA and EU
b) Top 3-5 schools in your country 
    b1) in KSA that would be KFUPM, KSU,          MBSC, KAU and Alfaisal University 

2. 90% GPA:

Self explanatory, take your GPA format (5.0 or 4.0) and x0.9 - this is your target.

3. Extracurricular Activities: 

Non of the “managed a book club, head of student council, barista at Starbucks” bullshit. Consulting internships, consulting competitions, hackathons, etc. Are what matters most.

4. Experience (for experienced hires):

Prior MBB experience is a massive plus, but not your only way in. “Unique” experience is what they look for in professionals who are shifting from industry. 

An ex-founder with a startup that failed before Series-B is more in-demand than an accountant in some commercial bank. 

5. Case interview performance: 

This is where most people fail. 

A bizzare brain teaser like “how many gas stations are in Riyadh” or “How many tooth brushes are in Dubai” may seem like an arbitrary question that measures nothing. It isn’t. It measures how quickly can you sort this problem into clean buckets and identify its drivers. Your contextual assumptions, your math, your final answer don’t matter. Only your ability to structure your thoughts does. 

And let’s be honest, it’s also a way to measure how quickly you can bullshit your way into a plausible-sounding answer when you’re put on the spot by a client.

As for the case itself, https://t.co/c7GHn0aDF7 is your best friend. Target solving 2 cases of each type CORRECTLY -however many tries it takes you- before interviewing.

I hope this is helpful to you whether you’re a student, fresh grad, or an experienced professional looking into shifting your career.

And thanks to @The_Lazy_Nerd for starting this.

MiMo-V2.6: The Hard Road to Scaling Up RL

MiMo-V2.6 is very likely one of the largest single RL runs, by compute, that any open-source model team has undertaken to date. In an era when compute is brutally scarce, we still chose to dedicate a team of several dozen people to one goal over an extended period: scaling up RL. That takes more than research conviction. It takes a vision for AGI, respect for the unknown, and the nerve to walk straight into the hardest problems.

The result is a model whose potential was built through mid-training and unlocked through heavy RL. Today, it is the number one open-source model. I strongly recommend reading the technical report. I believe it will become one of those papers that Agent RL practitioners keep reopening and discovering something new in each time. In my view, the research innovations and engineering challenges behind it surpass those of DeepSeek R1, which I was partly involved in.

Some will ask: why MixRL instead of MOPD? First, they are not competing choices. We ran MixRL on verifiable tasks of moderate difficulty, including code and related agentic tasks, and found that the resulting models generalize remarkably well. Second, tasks that are difficult to verify, extremely long-horizon, or simply too challenging to include in a joint RL run are trained separately. Including them would substantially reduce rollout efficiency or introduce significant rollout staleness. We then merge the resulting capabilities through MOPD. Games, 3D tasks, and tasks with subjective evaluation signals all fall into this category.

There is also a third, slightly cheeky answer. Our team is flat enough and free enough of organizational silos that MixRL simply is not difficult for us. More importantly, everyone enjoys working this way. People from different domains come together every day, driven by the pursuit of AGI and intelligence that can continuously improve itself, to confront and resolve the RL bottlenecks in each field. I will always remember the RL daily update meetings from this period. They were intense and dense, with intelligence emerging in real time.

To help the open-source community focus on solving real Agentic RL problems, we have released a Qwen model distilled from MiMo RL trajectories as a stronger starting point for RL, along with 7K diverse environments and a complete RL training framework. We hope these resources will help move Agentic RL research forward.

MiMo-V2.6 is only the beginning. In an era when intelligence is easy to replicate, we still choose the hard road toward self-improvement and AGI. Much of what lies ahead remains unknown. But we are willing to keep investing the time, compute, and passion required to take on one hard problem after another and work each of them all the way through, until intelligence crosses into a new regime.

Muse, Instinct, OpenClaw, Claude Code…
All successful agents have 3 key components:

🧠 Brain → model, harness (logic)
👐 Hands → tools, computer, browser
🗃️ Files → memories, skills, repos

The 'easy' way is to throw all these in 1 stateful computer (a Mac Mini)

Like, you run 𝚌𝚕𝚊𝚞𝚍𝚎 or 𝚏𝚡 in your mac, you keep it running all day with 𝚌𝚊𝚏𝚏𝚎𝚒𝚗𝚊𝚝𝚎, it has storage, and CLIs and apps installed.

But if you want to cost-efficiently run agents in the cloud, you actually start breaking down these parts.

🧠 The harness can run in Fluid compute. To make it reliable across restarts, rollouts, crashes, you make its event log durable using Workflow.

👐 The hands can be a dedicated browser fleet like Browserbase/Kernel, a computer like Sandbox, and even more efficient lightweight tools like just-bash.

🗃️ 🆕 What was missing was a way to also decouple storage. Imagine you want to run a memory consolidation cron job every night ("dreaming"). You can read/write to the files directly without 'booting up' the agent's full computer.

Today we're introducing the perfect companion to Sandbox: Drives. We shipped the computer for agents, now we're giving you the 'external disk' you can attach at will. It's early, and we'll be expanding capabilities here quickly.

Btw, breaking apart the agent into these independent parts not only optimizes costs in a big way, it also *massively* improves security and auditability. I'd argue you can't even run a secure agent otherwise!

how to improve GPT-6 Astra / Codex's ability to design and code websites

I've been using this approach since GPT Image was released, and the results have kept improving with 2 and 2.5

the idea is to have Codex generate visual mockups of the website before building it, whether you're reimagining an existing page or starting with an idea from scratch

you can review the layout, give feedback and agree on the design before it starts writing the frontend

here's how to use it:

1. give Codex the idea and your context

explain who the website is for, what it needs to communicate and what you want someone to do when they visit

include the material you already have:

> your page copy and product information
> brand guidelines, fonts, colors and assets
> screenshots of the existing page if you're redesigning
> references with notes on what you like about each one

have it ask about anything missing before generating the mockup

for an existing website, ask it to inspect the current implementation too, including components and functionality that need to stay

2. ask it to generate the design first

be explicit that you want an image mockup to review before implementation

a starting prompt:

> use imagegen to create a website mockup from this brief and the attached references
> use the supplied copy, brand assets and product information
> show the page layout, typography, imagery and calls to action, and wait for my feedback before writing code

you can request different visual directions if you're still exploring, with each version changing something meaningful like the layout or use of imagery

3. work through the mockup together

review it as a page someone needs to understand and use

> is the main message clear?
> does the layout guide attention toward the intended action?
> is the text readable?
> does the design fit your brand?
> are there generic sections or invented details that should be removed?

give specific feedback on the image, such as increasing the space around the headline, reducing decorative elements or moving the product example higher on the page

ask it to revise the chosen mockup while preserving the parts you've approved

4. turn the approved mockup into a build plan

have Codex identify the sections, reusable components and assets needed to implement the design

agree on what happens when someone interacts with it, including navigation, forms, buttons and any loading or error states

also define how the layout should adapt to mobile, because a desktop mockup leaves those decisions open

save the approved image and your decisions in the project so Codex can refer to them during the build

5. find relevant UX / UI skills before building

you can find these in skill directories and through recommendations on X, UI Skills is one example to explore

https://t.co/NSjtzraOfs

give your Grok Bot the project brief and have it research which skills are popular and worth considering for your stack

ask it to check what each skill does, who maintains it and whether its instructions fit the website you're building

that could include skills for:

> frontend design and component patterns
> accessibility and responsive layouts
> animation and interaction design
> reviewing the finished UI

review the shortlist, then give Codex the selected skills alongside your design system and approved mockup before implementation

6. build the page from that reference

ask Codex to implement the approved design using your project's existing stack and components where appropriate

keep headings, buttons and forms as working website elements, with illustrations and other generated visuals saved as separate assets

a useful implementation prompt:

> build the approved mockup as a responsive page

We believe we will look back on Astra as a turning point in how creatives use AI in video work.

For many months we were experimenting with different AI video approaches: generative workflows in ComfyUI, procedural animation with Python, motion design through the Cavalry and After Effects MCPs, and more. 

All of these were fundamentally limited by a lack of control. Generative models could sometimes make cool images, but changing one thing without disturbing everything else was difficult. 

Many of these generative tools weren't (and still aren't) built for true professional workflows. 

On the other hand, general models starting around Opus 4.5 were decent at writing python code to deterministically edit images and videos, but the models were really bad at “seeing” the images and videos they were supposed to be editing, which made them impractical.

The day Astra launched, just from the rumors and marketing, our internal sense was "this might be the one". Then, when we saw the level of 3D detail people were able to achieve with Astra in Blender, we really suspected the model was finally able to "see" and iterate toward things that actually looked good. 

While everyone raced to build cool (but often useless) demos of 3D worlds, we got interested in something else: compositing 3D assets into live action footage at commercial-grade quality. To this day, we are quite surprised by how few Astra demos focus on this ability. It feels like a breakthrough for us.

We tested a range of processes, from traditional VFX skills like masking and tracking to hybrid approaches like compositing Blender renders and generative imagery with real footage.

At the highest levels, Astra doesn’t replace someone with true domain expertise in VFX artistry. But, through these tests, it started to feel for the first time that the LLM was actually a viable tool in the kit. It worked well in concert with other tools to make professional results we could actually see ourselves using.

The coolest part about all this is that it makes it easy and painless to attempt visual effects on even the smallest projects and most off the cuff videos. I am genuinely worried that Google could lose the internet’s most valuable tollbooth over the next several years if it does not get its act together.

Amazon blocking Meta’s Muse agent is a huge warning about where the internet is heading. Amazon publicly cited privacy, security and authorization concerns but it also acknowledged that outside agents can bypass parts of its personalized shopping experience. Amazon is developing its own shopping agents, so allowing Muse to control product discovery and purchasing could hand Meta the most valuable part of the transaction, the customer relationship. That is the real battle in an agentic world. Today, people search for something, scroll through advertisements, open several links, compare their options and complete the transaction themselves. Tomorrow, a person will simply tell an AI agent what they want and let it research the products, compare prices and complete the purchase.

The agent could collapse ten searches, several advertisements and multiple website visits into a single conversation. That threatens every business that makes money by standing between a consumer’s question and the final transaction, but nobody has more to lose than Google. Google generated $60.4 billion from Search and other advertising during the first quarter of 2026, representing roughly 55% of Alphabet’s total revenue. Total Google advertising revenue reached approximately $77.3 billion, or around 70% of the company’s revenue.

Google’s business works because billions of high intent searches create valuable advertising inventory. Advertisers bid to appear when someone searches for a credit card, hotel, insurance policy, restaurant or product because those users are often close to spending money. If consumers begin asking Muse to make those decisions for them, Google does not merely lose a search, itcan lose the advertisement, the click, the behavioral data and eventually the transaction. Amazon’s decision to block Muse shows that the largest internet companies understand this danger. The company controlling the agent can decide which products get recommended, which merchants receive the order and which payment system processes the transaction. That position could eventually become more valuable than owning the website the agent visits.

Google Search currently looks stronger than ever. The chart shows Search revenue growth accelerating from 9.8% in early 2025 to 19.1% in early 2026, while Alphabet subsequently reported that first-quarter Search revenue increased 19% to $60.4 billion. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode are increasing Search usage rather than cannibalizing it and management reported that queries reached an all time high. However, the financial damage from a platform shift often appears after consumer behavior has already begun changing. AI generated answers are already reducing the need to click traditional search results. One 2026 study found that the first organic result’s click through rate fell from 20.02% to 9.69% when an AI Overview appeared, while a randomized field experiment found that AI Overviews reduced outbound organic clicks by 38%. Organic clicks are not the same as paid advertisements, so this does not prove that Google’s advertising revenue is about to collapse. However, it demonstrates the broader behavioral shift, users increasingly receive an answer without visiting the underlying websites. Agents take that shift one step further by completing the action without requiring the user to browse at all.

Google therefore faces an uncomfortable conflict. It must replace traditional Search with a more direct AI experience before competitors do, but every query it converts into one synthesized answer creates fewer obvious places to display the familiar list of advertisements. Google can insert advertisements into AI Mode and build agent driven shopping tools, but it still needs to prove that one AI conversation can monetize as effectively as an entire search results page. If it cannot, AI could improve the user experience while weakening the economics of the business.

Google clearly understands the threat, but it does not feel like the company is setting the direction of the consumer AI market. ChatGPT owns much of the mindshare, Claude is becoming a leading platform for coding and professional work, and Meta’s Muse is showing early momentum as an agent that can move across applications and complete real tasks. Google has Gemini and enormous distribution but it still has not produced a consumer agent with the same cultural momentum. It often feels like Google is responding to the industry rather than forcing everyone else to respond to it. The talent losses make this concern more serious. Over the past year, 25% of departing DeepMind researchers and advanced engineers reportedly moved to Anthropic, 21% went to Meta and 14% joined OpenAI. DeepMind’s ratio of arrivals to departures reportedly fell from approximately 12 to 1 in 2023 to roughly 2 to 1 in 2026.. Those departures reportedly include Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer, AlphaFold leader and Nobel laureate John Jumper, and Gemini contributors Jonas Adler and Alexander Pritzel.

Google still possesses some of the strongest assets in technology because it owns Android, Chrome, Search, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, Google Pay, Cloud and one of the world’s most accomplished AI research organizations. I interviewed every person we hired at @Clay in my orgs until we passed 300 people. 

We're scaling beyond that now, so our recruiting ops team built a system that keeps me involved in every hire. 

We have a Slack channel called hiring-theses and I review it every day. Before we hire anyone, the hiring manager writes a hiring thesis about the candidate. It answers four questions:

1. Why should we hire this person?
2. What is one exceptional thing this candidate has accomplished in their career or otherwise?
3. What are the risks/concerns?
4. How will we support this person if they join?

A thesis draws on a deep dive interview into the candidate's whole story, behavioral interviews, scored feedback from every round, and thorough reference calls. The thesis also includes every piece of submitted interviewer feedback. When I review that feedback, I notice discrepancies, pieces of feedback from an interviewer that the hiring manager didn't address, or missing voices I want to hear from. 

Then I approve, deny or discuss with the hiring team. I can't sit in every interview anymore, but I still read every thesis and every piece of feedback before someone joins Clay. 

Hopefully this is helpful to other teams scaling past the point where a founder can meet every candidate. Let me know if you have any questions!

Early takeaways from Austin Deep Tech Week: 

1. Austin is a serious f*cking city.

SF is still the center of gravity.

LA has built an absolute monster around aerospace, defense and industrials.

But after spending a few days in Austin, I'm increasingly convinced this city has structural advantages that the coasts underestimate.

People I've met here seem to have one primary objective:

Build.

Heads down. Gas pedal pinned to the floor.

Noticeably less obsession with looking important and more obsession with actually making shit work.

Deep tech rewards exactly that mentality.

2. Texas being aggressively pro-business isn't some Twitter talking point. It's an actual competitive advantage.

Heard versions of this repeatedly from founders and investors this week.

Permitting. Regulation. Taxes. Energy. Land. Manufacturing. Expansion.

When you're building software, you can abstract yourself away from geography.

When you're building atoms, geography becomes part of your cap table.

Every additional month waiting on a facility, permit, power connection or expansion is effectively dilution.

Texas understand that speed matters.

3. The coastal migration isn't over.

SF and LA still have unbelievable technical talent density, particularly at the earliest stages.

But the requirements change when a deep tech company starts working.

Now you need 100,000 square feet.

Power.

Testing.

Manufacturing.

Suppliers.

Technicians.

Hundreds of employees.

Suddenly Texas starts looking a hell of a lot more attractive.

And founders here don't seem nearly as worried about convincing talent to follow them as outsiders assume.

4. The next chapter isn't companies moving to Texas. It's companies starting here.

Historically the playbook has often been:

Coast → prove technology → raise capital → expand into Texas.

I think that increasingly becomes:

Texas → Texas → Texas.

More technical founders will move here before starting the company.

More pre-seed and seed companies will originate here.

More headquarters will be planted here from Day 1.

And that's when the flywheel gets interesting:

Talent → startups → capital → exits → experienced operators → new startups.

Once that loop starts compounding, ecosystems become very difficult to stop.

5. Austin feels significantly less distracted.

There is obviously bullshit everywhere. Startups attract grift like flies to shit.

But there's noticeably less keeping-up-with-the-Joneses energy here.

Less worrying about who raised what round.

Less optimizing for appearances.

Less obsession with which VC follows you or which dinner you got invited to.

More:

Does the thing actually work?

That cultural difference matters more than people realize.

6. “But the capital is on the coasts” is becoming a lazy argument.

Have you ever heard of a f*cking airplane?

It's 2026.

If you're building a generational company in Austin and a great investor in SF wants into the round, they're getting on the plane.

Great companies don't travel to capital.

Capital travels to great companies.

Austin already has serious institutional capital on the ground alongside a growing ecosystem of smaller funds.

More capital will follow the companies.

It always does.

7. Austin increasingly looks built for where deep tech is going, not where venture has been.

Deep tech is becoming less about a handful of scientists sitting in a Bay Area lab and increasingly about deploying massive amounts of physical infrastructure.

Factories.

Energy.

Robotics.

Defense.

Space.

Advanced manufacturing.

Data centers.

Industrial systems.

Those businesses eventually collide with the physical world.

And the physical world cares about land, power, regulation, labor, logistics and speed.

Texas has a lot of all six.

SF still has the deepest venture ecosystem. LA has built an extraordinary deep tech machine.

But Austin doesn't need to become either of them.

It may be building something fundamentally different:

A startup ecosystem optimized not just for inventing hard technology — but for actually industrializing it.

That's a much more interesting proposition.

Came into Austin Deep Tech Week thinking this was an important emerging hard tech ecosystem.

Now thinking “emerging” might already be outdated.

Ingredients are here.

Talent is coming.

Capital will follow.

Unlike a lot of startup ecosystems I've visited, Austin feels like it actually wants you to build shit here.

That's a hell of a tailwind 🏭🇺🇸

Finally - mad props @Andercot, @CaitlinCloud9, @Jason_A_Scharf + many others for putting this together & making this a kickass week!

On what made pg great, c. 2009-2016:

- every person tends toward particular kinds of ideas. Someone might tilt toward ideas that are entertaining, or elegant, or useful. Pg tended toward ideas that are surprising. He would look for surprising observations, generate surprising hypotheses, select surprising inferences. He'd never put it this way, but he seemed to find a lot of alpha in surprise
- pg was averse to abstractions. He almost always preferred a concrete way of doing things. Investors might ask about products or markets or business models. Pg would ask "what are you building?", "who is it for?", "how much will you charge?" It's the same questions, but he'd be as concrete and plain as possible
- being a hacker, he made things. His ideas were always practical and embodied in books, essays, software, YC, etc. They were meant to be used. It's very difficult to imagine pg writing a treatise on ethics or the nature of time or smtg
- this ethos is very much from Unix/C school of thought. Ironically, Pg was a Common Lisp hacker who embodied the worse-is-better philosophy. He would find the minimal possible thing that solves the problem, and it would be unmistakingly pg-esque. (If you haven't read The Rise of Worse is Better essay you should. Will the thesis be relitigated as AIs get much better?)
- that said, I'm not entirely sure he himself cared about making something people want. His output seems like an exhaust product of his curiosity that turned out to be useful by accident. Then again, he just couldn't help himself but stumble upon such accidents. Perhaps his way of thinking produces things people want, so for pg the score takes care of itself. The rest of us have to work at it deliberately
- he delighted in his ideas. The word "arrogance" has negative connotations, but pg was arrogant in the best possible way. If he thought an idea or an argument is good, it filled him with delight. It would then go into canon and he had no interest in revisiting it. There was no moving him once that happened
- the slop version of this is he "trusted his process" but again he would never put it this way. I don't think he was capable of navel gazing. It's impossible to imagine pg considering whether he'd be a favorite of fortune, or what posterity will think of him, or what he thinks of himself. In pg, the brain cycles most people spend on this would go to object level ideas
- I never saw the slightest sign he cares about what people think of him, nor did I ever see him try to impress anyone. I don't think he suppressed this impulse by force of will; as best as I could tell he has no such impulse. There is a Conversations with Tyler episode where pg keeps answering "I don't know" to a series of erudite questions without any embarrassment whatsoever. This is very pg
- he was interested in you if he thought you're smart and ambitious. If you did something to disabuse him of this, he'd lose interest completely. But this was never permanent; if you showed evidence of being smart and ambitious again his interest would rekindle. (You only got so many strikes, though) This brought out greatness in ppl because they would try very hard to impress him
- at the same time he genuinely cared about people's wellbeing. There are many stories where ppl had trouble in their personal life and he'd extend himself to help. I experienced some of this myself. Some values were much more important to him than ideas or ambition
- Thomas Jefferson once wrote "I am of a sect by myself", which I think sums up pg's character really well. If you read enough founding-father bios, you start noticing that most Silicon Valley figures resemble one founder more than the others. Imo pg is very much Jeffersonian

"I think a lot of starting startups is premature optimization. I see it in a lot of kids now, where they're part of a group and a lot of their friends are raising a lot of money, and some of them are becoming unicorns."

"The motivation becomes envy, a really negative motivation as opposed to a positive one."

"They pre-commit to an idea they're not even interested in, raise money for it, and start pre-optimizing for some path that they haven't really reached yet. That's why I always come back to this idea of curiosity. What is actually driving you?"

"Once you find that idea that you want to dedicate your life to, or dedicate the next 10 years to, it's going to have such gravity that you're not going to be able to avoid it."

"I actively tried not to start Replit, but it exploded into a startup on its own. That's the feeling you should get: 'I guess I have to do it,' because there's so much momentum behind it."

"There's a predatory thing I've heard that happens right now where VCs go to Stanford students and give them a million dollars pre-idea... It's like the music industry... You're taking this young person and pre-committing them to something they shouldn't have committed to."

@amasad

Replit co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad says the job of young people is to be heretics and question society's deeply held beliefs:

"What is college, and what is it for? A related question is: What is the utility of young people in society?"

"We probably have a blind spot in society. We have a lot of blind spots in Silicon Valley. There are a lot of ideas that don't come out of Silicon Valley because there's a monoculture here."

"There's a certain way of thinking. Every culture is somehow a monoculture, even the most radical cultures like Silicon Valley."

"What do you need from young people? You need them to experiment. You need to encourage them to try impossible things."

"Every now and then, they're going to have a breakthrough that once we thought was impossible, and now it's suddenly possible because the technology changed, something changed."

"College ultimately should be about that. Let's get these people with clear minds, Zen mindsets, first-principles mindsets, and encourage them to question the deeply held beliefs."

Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR.

We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.
